title: State v. Gleason
description: Whether the Kansas Constitution's "inviolate" jury trial right requires automatic reversal for instructional errors omitting an element of a criminal offense, or if such errors are subject to a harmless error analysis.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the Court of Appeals wrongly reversed Gleason's conviction, contending that most prosecutorial comments were within wide latitude, the single prosecutorial error was harmless, and the jury instruction error (omitting an element) was also harmless because the State rebutted the presumption of prejudice by showing Gleason was not prejudiced.
defendant_argument: Gleason argued that the prosecutorial errors and the jury instruction error (omitting an element) warranted reversal. He specifically claimed that the "inviolate" jury trial right under Section 5 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights precludes any harmless error analysis for such instructional errors, demanding automatic reversal.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' judgment and affirmed the district court's judgment, thereby upholding Gleason's conviction.

title: State v. Stubbs
description: Whether K.S.A. 21-6301(a)(2), which prohibits possessing a "dangerous knife" with intent to use it "unlawfully against another," is unconstitutionally vague due to a lack of meaningful enforcement standards, thereby impermissibly delegating legislative power.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Kansas argued that K.S.A. 21-6301(a)(2) provides adequate enforcement guidelines, particularly with its definition of a "dangerous knife" and the intent requirement, to prevent arbitrary enforcement.
defendant_argument: Brian S. Stubbs argued that the criminal-use-of-weapons statute is unconstitutionally vague because the term "dangerous knife" lacks meaningful enforcement standards, giving too much discretion to police, prosecutors, and judges.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Brian S. Stubbs' convictions, ruling that the criminal-use-of-weapons statute is not unconstitutionally vague and that there was sufficient evidence to support his interference-with-law-enforcement conviction.

title: State v. Phipps
description: Whether the completion of a criminal sentence renders an appeal moot, thereby extinguishing the court's jurisdiction to review the case, and whether "prudential exceptions" to mootness are constitutionally permissible in Kansas.
plaintiff_argument: Phipps argued that his case was not moot because the issues presented were of statewide importance and capable of repetition, and therefore, the court should review his challenge to his criminal history score.
defendant_argument: The State also argued that the case was not moot due to the statewide importance and repetitive nature of the issues, and that the Court of Appeals correctly affirmed Phipps' sentence based on Counterman.
decision_outcome: The court dismissed the appeal, ruling that Phipps' completion of his sentence rendered the case moot, and explicitly overruled prior caselaw that allowed for "prudential exceptions" to mootness, holding that once an issue is moot, jurisdiction is extinguished.

title: State v. Green
description: Whether the premeditated first-degree murder statute is unconstitutionally vague, whether the district court erred in excluding preliminary hearing testimony of an allegedly unavailable witness, and whether Green knowingly and intelligently waived his right to counsel at sentencing.
plaintiff_argument: The premeditated first-degree murder statute is unconstitutionally vague, the district court erred by not admitting a witness's preliminary hearing testimony based on counsel's statements of unavailability, and Green's waiver of counsel at sentencing was invalid due to an intervening event requiring a new colloquy.
defendant_argument: The premeditated first-degree murder statute is not unconstitutionally vague, Green failed to provide sufficient evidence to establish witness unavailability, and Green's initial waiver of counsel remained valid as no substantial change in circumstances occurred to require a new waiver at sentencing.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Green's convictions and sentence, finding no error in the district court's rulings on the premeditated first-degree murder statute's constitutionality, witness unavailability, or the waiver of counsel.

title: Kansas v. Harper
description: Whether the Kansas Department of Revenue (KDOR) must cease its practice of allowing gender reclassification on driver's licenses based on the Attorney General's interpretation of K.S.A. 77-207.
plaintiff_argument: The Attorney General argued that K.S.A. 77-207 requires the KDOR to list biological sex at birth on driver's licenses, asserting that "sex" and "gender" are synonymous in the statute, and that the Court of Appeals erred in its standards for irreparable injury and likelihood of prevailing on the merits.
defendant_argument: The KDOR and Intervenors argued that the KDOR is not violating K.S.A. 77-207, as its data set maintains original sex at birth while allowing gender reclassification on physical licenses, and that "sex" and "gender" are not synonymous, or that the statute is ambiguous and allows for discretion.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court denied the petition for review, upholding the Court of Appeals' decision to reverse the temporary injunction against the Kansas Department of Revenue's policy of allowing gender reclassification on driver's licenses and remanding the case to a new judge.

title: Hodes & Nauser v. Kobach; Hodes & Nauser v. Stanek
description: Whether a series of state statutes and regulations relating to the licensure of abortion provider facilities are constitutional under section 1 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights.
plaintiff_argument: The Challenged Laws infringe on a woman's fundamental right to personal autonomy, including the right to abortion, and do not survive strict scrutiny.
defendant_argument: The Challenged Laws are constitutional, do not infringe on the right to abortion, and serve compelling government interests in protecting maternal health and regulating the medical profession.
decision_outcome: The Kansas Supreme Court affirmed the district court's decision, striking down the Challenged Laws as unconstitutional and issuing a permanent injunction against their enforcement.

title: League of Women Voters of Kansas v. Schwab
description: Whether three new Kansas election laws, concerning false representation as an election official, signature verification for advance ballots, and restrictions on ballot collection, violate various provisions of the Kansas Constitution, including rights to free speech, the right to vote, equal protection, and due process.
plaintiff_argument: The League of Women Voters of Kansas and others argued that the false representation provision violates free speech, the signature verification requirement violates the right to vote, equal protection, and due process, and the ballot collection restriction violates the right to vote and free speech.
defendant_argument: Scott Schwab (Secretary of State) and Kris W. Kobach (Attorney General) argued that the laws are constitutional, with the false representation provision only regulating unprotected speech, the signature verification being a valid "proper proof" for electors, and ballot collection not constituting protected speech or expressive conduct.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the denial of a temporary injunction against the false representation provision, finding it likely unconstitutional as overbroad. It reversed the dismissal of claims against the signature verification requirement, remanding for review under equal protection and due process standards, but found the requirement itself a valid "proper proof" under Article 5. It affirmed the dismissal of claims against the ballot collection restriction, finding it neither an additional qualification on the right to vote nor an infringement on free speech.

title: City of Olathe v. City of Spring Hill
description: Whether an elected governing body can enter into an agreement that binds future governing bodies regarding annexation and development policies, thereby constraining their legislative power.
plaintiff_argument: The City of Olathe argued that the agreement was enforceable, authorized by K.S.A. 2021 Supp. 12-2908 concerning municipal contracts for governmental services and K.S.A. 12-101 enabling home-rule, and supported by precedent like Simmons.
defendant_argument: The City of Spring Hill argued that the agreement was an unenforceable attempt to bind future City Councils to governmental policy decisions, which is not authorized by law and undermines democratic principles.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's decision, ruling that the agreement between Olathe and Spring Hill was unenforceable as a governmental action that could not bind subsequent City Councils, and denied Olathe's request for injunctive relief.

title: In re Schmidt
description: Whether the legislative reapportionment of state senatorial and representative districts, as contained in Substitute for Senate Bill 563, is valid under state and federal law, with the Attorney General arguing for its validity and an intervenor senator arguing against it due to procedural flaws and unconstitutional district boundaries.
plaintiff_argument: The Attorney General, as the petitioner, argued that the legislative enactment (Substitute for Senate Bill 563) is valid and contains no constitutional errors, having followed proper procedures and substantive requirements.
defendant_argument: Intervenor Senator Thomas Holland argued that Substitute for Senate Bill 563 is invalid due to procedural irregularities in its enactment and that the new district boundaries are unconstitutional, citing issues like lack of compactness, contiguity, and alleged political gerrymandering.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the legislative enactment, Substitute for Senate Bill 563, is valid, upholding the reapportionment maps for state senatorial and representative districts.

title: Rivera v. Schwab
description: Whether the Kansas Legislature's congressional redistricting map, "Ad Astra 2," violates the Kansas Constitution by engaging in partisan and racial gerrymandering and diluting minority votes.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the "Ad Astra 2" redistricting map constitutes unconstitutional partisan and racial gerrymandering and dilutes minority votes, violating various provisions of the Kansas Constitution, including equal protection, free speech, and voting rights.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the "Ad Astra 2" map is constitutional, that state courts lack jurisdiction to review partisan gerrymandering claims, and that plaintiffs failed to prove racial gerrymandering or vote dilution under the correct legal standards.
decision_outcome: The Kansas Supreme Court reversed the district court's judgment, finding that the plaintiffs did not establish that the "Ad Astra 2" redistricting map violated the Kansas Constitution, and lifted the injunction.

title: State v. Carr
description: Whether the Kansas capital sentencing scheme violates Section 1 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights by infringing upon the right to life, which the plaintiff argues is absolute and nonforfeitable.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that Section 1 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights guarantees an absolute, nonforfeitable right to life, which precludes the state from imposing capital punishment.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that the natural right to life under Section 1 is forfeitable through criminal conduct, and thus the state's capital sentencing scheme does not unconstitutionally infringe upon this right.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Reginald Dexter Carr Jr.'s death sentence, concluding that the Kansas capital sentencing scheme does not violate Section 1 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights.

title: State v. Carr
description: Whether Kansas' capital sentencing scheme violates Section 1 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights, whether death qualification of jurors under K.S.A. 22-3410 violates Section 5 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights, and whether various penalty-phase errors warrant reversal of Jonathan D. Carr's death sentence.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the capital sentencing scheme and death qualification process are constitutional, and that any alleged penalty-phase errors were harmless and do not warrant reversal of the death sentence.
defendant_argument: Jonathan D. Carr argued that the Kansas death penalty scheme violates his right to life under the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights, that death qualification of jurors violates his right to a jury trial, and that numerous penalty-phase errors, including prosecutorial misconduct and improper jury instructions, cumulatively violated his rights and require reversal of his death sentence.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Jonathan D. Carr's death sentence, concluding he is not entitled to relief on the penalty-phase issues and that the evidence supports the aggravating circumstances outweighing mitigating circumstances.

title: State v. Brown
description: Whether the State's use of peremptory challenges was racially discriminatory, whether the Kansas Sentencing Guidelines Act (KSGA) violates the Kansas Constitution by allowing judges to determine criminal history for sentencing, and whether Kansas' criminal restitution scheme violates jury trial rights under the Sixth Amendment or the Kansas Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Brown argued that the State's peremptory challenges were racially motivated, violating equal protection; the KSGA violates section 5 of the Kansas Constitution by allowing judges to make criminal history findings for sentencing; and Kansas' criminal restitution scheme violates jury trial rights under the Sixth Amendment and section 5 of the Kansas Constitution because judges determine restitution damages.
defendant_argument: The State contended that Brown failed to prove intentional discrimination in peremptory challenges; the KSGA does not violate section 5 of the Kansas Constitution; and Kansas' criminal restitution scheme does not violate the Sixth Amendment, and while it implicates section 5, the offending provisions are severable.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Brown's convictions and the restitution order, but vacated his sentence and remanded the case for resentencing because his prior Michigan juvenile adjudication for armed robbery was erroneously classified as a person felony.

title: State v. Arnett
description: Whether Kansas's criminal restitution statutes violate the right to a jury trial under the Sixth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution and Section 5 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that criminal restitution does not violate the Sixth Amendment because it is not punishment, and even if it were, it does not increase the statutory maximum penalty. It also contended that criminal restitution and civil damages are separate remedies, thus not implicating Section 5 of the Kansas Constitution.
defendant_argument: Taylor Arnett argued that the criminal restitution statutes violate the Sixth Amendment because restitution is a form of punishment that increases the maximum penalty without a jury finding. She also contended that the statutes violate Section 5 because, historically, juries determined damages in civil cases and the value of stolen property in criminal cases, which is analogous to modern restitution.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the restitution order against Arnett, ruling that Kansas's criminal restitution statutes do not violate the Sixth Amendment. However, it found that the statutes do violate Section 5 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights insofar as they give restitution the effect of a civil judgment, and remedied this by severing the offending portions of the statutes.

title: State v. Robison
description: Whether the Kansas criminal restitution statutes violate the right to a jury trial under the Sixth Amendment of the United States Constitution or section 5 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights by allowing a judge to determine restitution amounts.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that criminal restitution is not a criminal punishment or is a distinct civil remedy, and therefore the statutes do not violate the right to a jury trial.
defendant_argument: Robison argued that the statutes violate his right to a jury trial because they allow a judge to determine damages (restitution), which should be decided by a jury, especially since modern restitution orders are treated like civil judgments.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's restitution order against Robison but found several Kansas criminal restitution statutes unconstitutional in part, severing the provisions that made criminal restitution orders equivalent to civil judgments enforceable without a jury trial.

title: State v. Albano
description: Whether the Kansas Sentencing Guidelines Act (KSGA) violates section 5 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights by allowing courts, rather than juries, to make criminal history findings for sentencing purposes.
plaintiff_argument: Albano argues that the KSGA violates section 5 because it allows the sentencing court, rather than a jury, to find prior convictions for sentencing, which she asserts was a common-law right preserved by section 5 at the time the Kansas Constitution was adopted.
defendant_argument: The State argues that Kansas law has long recognized the jury's role in determining guilt and the court's role in determining punishment, including prior convictions, and that the KSGA's method does not implicate the right to trial by jury.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeals and the district court, ruling that the KSGA provisions allowing courts to make criminal history findings for sentencing purposes do not violate section 5 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights.

title: Tillman v. Goodpasture
description: Whether K.S.A. 2020 Supp. 60-1906(a), which abolishes "wrongful birth" actions, violates the constitutional rights to a jury trial and a legal remedy under sections 5 and 18 of the Kansas Constitution Bill of Rights.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff parents argue that the statute abolishing wrongful birth actions is unconstitutional, violating their rights to a jury trial and a legal remedy, and that their doctor's negligence deprived them of the right to make an informed decision about terminating the pregnancy.
defendant_argument: The defendant and intervenor argue that the statute abolishing wrongful birth actions is constitutional because wrongful birth was a "new" tort not recognized at common law when the Kansas Constitution was adopted, and therefore sections 5 and 18 do not apply.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's decision, ruling that the statute abolishing wrongful birth actions is constitutional, thereby dismissing the parents' lawsuit.
